PHASE 7 · FNP CERTIFICATION REVIEW & CLINICAL INTEGRATION

Week 145 — Lesson 169: Diagnostic Testing & Laboratory Interpretation Board Review

FNP-level goal: Select tests that answer a defined clinical question, interpret results in the context of pretest probability and data quality, recognize time-sensitive abnormalities, integrate patterns rather than isolated flags, and ensure every result is communicated and acted upon safely.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish screening, diagnostic, confirmatory, monitoring, prognostic, and surveillance tests.
  • Use pretest probability, sensitivity, specificity, predictive value, and likelihood ratios conceptually.
  • Recognize preanalytic, analytic, and postanalytic sources of error.
  • Interpret common CBC, chemistry, kidney, liver, endocrine, urine, infectious, and cardiac patterns.
  • Identify results that require immediate verification, stabilization, escalation, or emergency referral.
  • Choose the least harmful test that can meaningfully change management.
  • Avoid false reassurance, incidental cascades, duplicate testing, and inappropriate broad panels.
  • Close the loop from order through specimen, result, communication, action, and follow-up.

Part 1 — Start With the Clinical Question

Before ordering a test, state what decision it should inform. Is the goal to detect disease in an asymptomatic population, confirm a suspected diagnosis, exclude a dangerous alternative, determine severity, guide treatment, monitor toxicity, assess response, or estimate prognosis?

A test without a decision pathway can generate data without improving care. The board-style question often asks for the next best test, not the largest panel or the most technologically advanced study.

Part 2 — Tests Do Not Replace History and Examination

Clinical data determine which test is appropriate and how the result should be interpreted. Onset, severity, vital signs, exposures, medications, pregnancy, immune status, comorbidity, and focused examination establish the pretest probability.

An unstable patient may need immediate treatment and transfer before definitive testing. A reassuring test cannot compensate for ignoring shock, respiratory failure, acute neurologic deficit, severe bleeding, or another time-sensitive syndrome.

Part 3 — Classify the Testing Purpose

  • Screening: evaluates an asymptomatic defined population.
  • Diagnostic: investigates symptoms, signs, or an abnormal screen.
  • Confirmatory: verifies a diagnosis when one result is insufficient.
  • Monitoring: follows disease, treatment response, or toxicity.
  • Surveillance: searches for recurrence or progression in a known-risk state.
  • Prognostic: estimates outcome or future risk.

The same analyte can serve different purposes, but the population, threshold, and consequences may differ.

Part 4 — Pretest Probability Changes Meaning

A positive result is more convincing when the disease was reasonably likely before testing. In a very low-risk population, even a good test can produce more false positives relative to true positives. In a very high-risk emergency, a negative result may not safely end evaluation if sensitivity, timing, or specimen quality is inadequate.

Estimate probability from prevalence, individual risk, and clinical findings. Do not treat a laboratory flag as a diagnosis independent of context.

Part 5 — Sensitivity and Specificity

Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the condition who test positive. A highly sensitive test can be useful for ruling out disease when negative if it was performed at the correct time and under validated conditions.

Specificity is the proportion without the condition who test negative. A highly specific test can help rule in disease when positive. These memory rules are useful only when the test and population fit the case.

Part 6 — Predictive Values Depend on Prevalence

Positive predictive value asks how often a positive result represents disease in the tested population. Negative predictive value asks how often a negative result represents absence of disease. Both change with prevalence and pretest probability.

This explains why a test can perform differently in a specialty clinic, emergency department, community screening event, and low-risk preventive population even when analytic sensitivity and specificity are unchanged.

Part 7 — Likelihood Ratios Update Probability

Positive and negative likelihood ratios describe how much a result shifts odds. A result with a large positive likelihood ratio meaningfully raises probability; one with a very small negative likelihood ratio meaningfully lowers it.

You may not need formal calculations on every question. Ask whether this result changes probability enough to cross a testing, treatment, referral, or emergency threshold.

Part 8 — Reference Interval Is Not a Diagnostic Boundary

A reference interval commonly describes values observed in a defined reference population. A value just outside it is not automatically disease, and a value inside it is not automatically safe. Laboratories, assays, units, age, sex-related biology, pregnancy, altitude, and population methods can change intervals.

Diagnostic and treatment thresholds are established for specific outcomes and may not match the laboratory's flag. Interpret the actual value, units, trend, and clinical state.

Part 9 — Preanalytic Error Happens Before Measurement

Wrong patient, wrong tube, mislabeling, prolonged tourniquet time, hemolysis, contamination, delayed transport, improper temperature, nonfasting state, posture, exercise, timing relative to medication, and poor specimen technique can distort results.

When a result is surprising, ask whether the specimen is credible. Repeat sampling may be appropriate, but a critical result compatible with illness should not be dismissed as error without immediate clinical assessment.

Part 10 — Analytic and Postanalytic Error

Analytic problems include assay interference, calibration, reagent, instrument, and method limitations. Postanalytic problems include incorrect routing, delayed review, transcription, unit confusion, failure to communicate, and failure to act.

Point-of-care testing is convenient but still requires approved use, quality control, trained personnel, correct technique, and awareness of limitations. A fast answer is not necessarily an accurate or definitive answer.

Part 11 — Verify Identity, Units, and Trend

Before reacting, verify the patient, collection time, reference interval, units, specimen status, prior values, and relevant medications. Compare the trajectory: acute change may matter more than one absolute value.

Beware of copied results, duplicated orders, and unit mismatches across systems. A creatinine reported in mg/dL cannot be compared directly with a value reported in micromoles per liter without conversion.

Part 12 — CBC: Interpret the Three Cell Lines

Read hemoglobin and hematocrit with red-cell indices, white-cell count with differential, and platelet count. Then ask whether one, two, or all three cell lines are abnormal.

Isolated anemia suggests a different framework from pancytopenia. A normal total white count can hide neutropenia or lymphocyte abnormalities, so the differential and absolute counts may be clinically important.

Part 13 — Anemia: Begin With MCV and Reticulocyte Response

Classify anemia as microcytic, normocytic, or macrocytic, then assess chronicity, bleeding, nutrition, kidney disease, inflammation, medications, hemolysis, marrow disease, pregnancy, and symptoms. The reticulocyte response helps distinguish underproduction from an appropriate marrow response to loss or destruction.

Microcytosis suggests iron-restricted erythropoiesis, thalassemia, and selected other causes; macrocytosis suggests vitamin deficiency, alcohol or liver disease, hypothyroidism, medications, reticulocytosis, or marrow disease. Do not prescribe iron solely because hemoglobin is low.

Part 14 — Iron Studies Are a Pattern

Ferritin reflects storage but also rises with inflammation. Transferrin saturation, serum iron, binding capacity, CBC indices, inflammation, kidney disease, and clinical history help distinguish absolute deficiency from inflammatory iron restriction.

Iron deficiency requires both treatment and evaluation of its cause when appropriate. In an adult without an obvious benign explanation, occult blood loss or malabsorption may require investigation.

Part 15 — White Cells and Infection

Leukocytosis can reflect infection, inflammation, stress, corticosteroids, smoking, pregnancy-related physiology, marrow disease, and other causes. Leukopenia can reflect viral illness, medications, autoimmune disease, marrow suppression, nutritional deficiency, or severe infection.

Do not diagnose bacterial infection from leukocytosis alone. Integrate symptoms, examination, differential, specimen evidence, imaging when indicated, and clinical trajectory.

Part 16 — Platelets and Coagulation

Thrombocytopenia can result from decreased production, destruction or consumption, sequestration, dilution, or laboratory artifact such as platelet clumping. Bleeding risk depends on count, trend, platelet function, anticoagulants, procedure, and clinical bleeding.

PT/INR and aPTT evaluate portions of coagulation under specific conditions but do not measure all bleeding or thrombotic risk. A markedly abnormal result, active bleeding, suspected DIC, or heparin-related syndrome may require urgent escalation.

Part 17 — Sodium: Ask About Water Balance

Sodium concentration primarily reflects water relative to sodium rather than total-body sodium alone. Evaluate severity, symptoms, duration, glucose, serum osmolality when relevant, volume status, urine studies, medications, kidney, heart, liver, adrenal, and thyroid context.

Seizure, severe confusion, coma, or rapid change is an emergency. Avoid rapid unplanned correction because neurologic injury can occur in both severe hyponatremia and hypernatremia.

Part 18 — Potassium Can Be an Electrical Emergency

Confirm unexpected hyperkalemia while immediately assessing symptoms, renal function, medications, hemolysis, and ECG when indicated. Pseudohyperkalemia can occur, but a compatible critical value or ECG abnormality demands urgent treatment rather than waiting casually for a repeat.

Hypokalemia also increases arrhythmia risk, especially with cardiac disease, digoxin, QT-prolonging conditions, or magnesium deficiency. Identify loss, shift, intake, and medication causes.

Part 19 — Bicarbonate and the Anion Gap

A low serum bicarbonate can reflect metabolic acidosis or compensation for respiratory alkalosis. A high bicarbonate can reflect metabolic alkalosis or compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis. Blood gas data and clinical context may be necessary.

The anion gap helps organize metabolic acidosis but is influenced by albumin and laboratory method. Do not stop after naming the disorder; identify the cause, severity, respiratory compensation, and need for emergency treatment.

Part 20 — Kidney Function Requires GFR and Albuminuria

Serum creatinine is influenced by filtration, muscle mass, diet, medications, and secretion. Estimated GFR is more informative than creatinine alone but still has limitations. Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio adds a separate dimension of kidney damage and cardiovascular risk.

KDIGO defines chronic kidney disease by abnormalities of kidney structure or function present for at least three months and classifies it by cause, GFR category, and albuminuria category. One abnormal value during acute illness does not establish chronicity.

Part 21 — Acute Kidney Injury Is a Trend and a Syndrome

Compare current and baseline creatinine, urine output, volume status, hemodynamics, medications, obstruction risk, urinalysis, and systemic features. Organize causes as prerenal perfusion, intrinsic kidney injury, and postrenal obstruction while recognizing overlap.

Urgent concerns include severe hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, severe acidosis, uremic complications, anuria, rapidly progressive findings, or obstruction with infection or solitary-kidney risk.

Part 22 — Liver Tests: Pattern Before Label

Aminotransferase-predominant elevation suggests a hepatocellular pattern; alkaline-phosphatase-predominant elevation suggests cholestatic or infiltrative disease after confirming hepatic source when needed. Bilirubin can be conjugated or unconjugated and has multiple causes.

Albumin and coagulation measures can reflect synthetic function but are influenced by nutrition, inflammation, anticoagulation, and other conditions. Marked injury, jaundice with systemic illness, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, or suspected obstruction requires expedited evaluation.

Part 23 — Glucose and A1C Answer Different Time Frames

Plasma glucose reflects the sampled moment; A1C estimates longer-term glycemic exposure. ADA 2026 criteria for nonpregnant individuals include A1C at least 6.5%, fasting plasma glucose at least 126 mg/dL, two-hour glucose at least 200 mg/dL during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test, or random plasma glucose at least 200 mg/dL with classic hyperglycemic symptoms or crisis.

Without unequivocal hyperglycemia, diagnosis requires confirmation. Conditions that alter red-cell turnover, some hemoglobin variants, pregnancy, dialysis, and other states can make A1C discordant; use appropriate plasma glucose criteria and investigate substantial discordance.

Part 24 — Thyroid Testing Is an Axis

TSH is usually the initial test for primary thyroid dysfunction in appropriate patients, with free T4 clarifying abnormal or discordant patterns. High TSH with low free T4 supports primary hypothyroidism; suppressed TSH with elevated thyroid hormone supports primary hyperthyroidism.

Central disease, pregnancy, severe nonthyroidal illness, biotin and other assay interference, medications, and timing can alter interpretation. Do not diagnose or dose-adjust from a single unexpected result without context.

Part 25 — Urinalysis: Chemistry Plus Microscopy Plus Symptoms

Dipstick, microscopy, and culture provide different information. Leukocyte esterase and nitrite can support urinary inflammation or bacteriuria but do not diagnose symptomatic infection alone. Contamination, collection quality, menstruation, hydration, and timing matter.

Do not culture or treat asymptomatic bacteriuria indiscriminately. Pregnancy and selected urologic procedures are important exceptions under current guidance. Hematuria, casts, protein, or persistent abnormalities may indicate a noninfectious renal or urologic pathway.

Part 26 — Microbiology Depends on the Specimen

Obtain cultures from the correct site with proper technique and, when feasible, before antibiotics. A positive molecular test may detect nucleic acid without proving active disease in every context; a culture may reflect colonization or contamination rather than infection.

Interpret organism, quantity, specimen quality, host, syndrome, prior therapy, and susceptibility report together. Diagnostic stewardship improves antimicrobial stewardship.

Part 27 — Inflammatory Markers Are Nonspecific

ESR and CRP can support assessment of inflammation and trends but rarely establish a diagnosis alone. They may be normal in important disease or elevated from infection, autoimmune disease, malignancy, tissue injury, pregnancy, age, obesity, and other conditions.

Use them only when the result will affect probability, monitoring, or management. Avoid serial testing without a defined clinical purpose.

Part 28 — Troponin and Natriuretic Peptides Need Context

Troponin indicates myocardial injury, not automatically type 1 myocardial infarction. Interpret symptoms, ECG, serial change, assay-specific threshold, timing, kidney disease, tachyarrhythmia, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, and other causes.

BNP or NT-proBNP can support heart-failure evaluation but is affected by age, kidney function, body composition, rhythm, and other cardiac stress. Biomarkers complement rather than replace clinical assessment and imaging.

Part 29 — Imaging Has Pretest and Harm Considerations

Select imaging by clinical question, urgency, sensitivity, radiation, contrast risk, pregnancy, availability, cost, and whether the finding changes management. Ultrasound, radiography, CT, MRI, and nuclear studies answer different questions.

A more sensitive scan can also detect incidental findings that trigger cascades. Use validated appropriateness guidance and do not image uncomplicated conditions without red flags simply because technology is available.

Part 30 — Incidental Findings Need Proportional Response

First verify what was found, how confidently it was characterized, comparison with prior studies, patient risk, and the radiologist or laboratory recommendation. Then distinguish benign no-action findings from those needing surveillance, dedicated imaging, or referral.

Avoid both neglect and panic. Explain uncertainty and create a traceable follow-up plan with a named owner.

Part 31 — Critical Results and Diagnostic Safety

For a critical or unexpected result, assess the patient rather than the number alone. Confirm identity and specimen credibility, contact the patient using an escalation pathway, direct emergency care when indicated, document communication, and ensure handoff acceptance.

Portal release does not replace clinician responsibility. AHRQ describes closed-loop care as ensuring results are sent, received, acknowledged, communicated understandably, and acted upon.

Part 32 — Common Board-Style Testing Traps

  • Ordering a broad panel before forming a differential
  • Using a screening test for a symptomatic patient
  • Choosing definitive testing before stabilization
  • Treating a laboratory flag as a diagnosis
  • Ignoring timing, specimen quality, or assay interference
  • Failing to confirm a diagnosis when required
  • Repeating a test that cannot change management
  • Missing a critical trend because the value remains inside the reference interval
  • Ordering a test without planning follow-up

Clinical Case 1 — The Hemolyzed Potassium

A patient with CKD taking an ACE inhibitor has weakness and a potassium of 6.8 mEq/L reported from a hemolyzed specimen. The learner assumes the value is false and schedules a repeat next week.

Reasoning: Hemolysis can falsely elevate potassium, but patient risk and symptoms make the result potentially dangerous. Assess immediately, obtain an ECG and urgent repeat using a reliable specimen, and treat or transfer without delay if hyperkalemia or electrical toxicity is present.

Clinical Case 2 — Anemia Is Not Automatically Iron Deficiency

An older adult has fatigue, hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, macrocytosis, neuropathic symptoms, and long-term metformin use. The learner prescribes iron without further evaluation.

Reasoning: Classify the anemia and investigate macrocytosis, vitamin B12 risk, reticulocyte response, medications, thyroid and liver context, alcohol exposure, and marrow disease as appropriate. Iron should not be selected from hemoglobin alone.

Clinical Case 3 — Discordant A1C

A patient with anemia and recent blood loss has fasting glucose repeatedly in the diabetic range but an A1C that appears only mildly elevated.

Reasoning: Red-cell turnover can distort A1C. Use appropriate plasma glucose criteria, confirm as required, and investigate the discordance rather than allowing the A1C to overrule credible glucose data.

Clinical Case 4 — The Unowned Result

A CT ordered during an urgent visit shows an incidental pulmonary nodule. The result is released to the portal, but no clinician documents review or assigns follow-up.

Reasoning: Automatic release is not closed-loop care. Risk-stratify using the report and current guidance, communicate the finding and uncertainty, arrange the indicated follow-up, and assign responsibility for tracking completion.

FNP High-Yield Framework: TRACE

  1. T — Target the question: Screening, diagnosis, exclusion, severity, monitoring, prognosis, or toxicity.
  2. R — Risk and red flags: Stability, pretest probability, life stage, comorbidity, medications, and consequence of delay.
  3. A — Assay and acquisition: Right test, timing, specimen, units, quality, limitations, interference, and prior values.
  4. C — Contextualize the pattern: Trends, related results, physiology, differential, thresholds, and what the result changes.
  5. E — Escalate and ensure closure: Stabilize, repeat, treat, refer, communicate, document, track, and reassess.

Take-Home Summary

Begin testing with a clinical question and a patient stability assessment. Classify the test's purpose, estimate pretest probability, and select the least harmful study likely to change management. Interpret sensitivity, specificity, predictive value, reference intervals, specimen quality, units, trends, assay limitations, and related patterns rather than reacting to isolated flags. Read the CBC by cell line, anemia by indices and marrow response, chemistry by water and acid-base physiology, kidney disease by chronicity plus eGFR and albuminuria, liver tests by injury pattern and function, glucose and A1C by time frame and interference, thyroid tests as an axis, and urine or microbiology results in the syndrome and specimen context. Critical values require patient assessment, verification without unsafe delay, and escalation. Every test needs an owner from order through communication and action.

Educational note: This lesson is educational and does not replace current laboratory reference information, assay instructions, clinical guidelines, local critical-value policy, consultation, or emergency evaluation. Thresholds and methods can change and may differ by laboratory and patient population. Verify current ADA, KDIGO, FDA, CDC, AHRQ, specialty, laboratory, and institutional guidance before clinical use.
